title: Go, From Zero
intro: Go is a small language built almost entirely out of arguments about what to leave out. This week goes from an empty file to goroutines, stopping at the three or four places where Go behaves differently from what your instincts predict — and explaining why it was designed that way, because the reason is usually the part worth remembering. Everything here runs with nothing but the Go toolchain installed.

days.title: Hello, and a compiler that says no
days.teaser: An unused variable is a build error, and the rule everyone calls a language rule technically isn't one
days.teachBack: Go refuses to compile a program containing an unused variable or an unused import. Give both of the separate motives behind that decision — one about your bugs, one about everybody's build times — and explain why the escape hatch was deliberately made ugly rather than convenient.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Go is a small language. That is not marketing — the spec is about 100 pages, it has 25
keywords, and you can hold most of it in your head. C++ has 90-odd keywords and a
standard nobody has read end to end. The whole design is a series of arguments about what
to *leave out*, and the fastest way to understand Go is to keep asking "what did they
refuse to add, and why".

Today: getting a program to run, and meeting the two refusals that make newcomers
furious in week one and grateful in month three.

### The smallest program that works

```go order
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("hello from Go")
}
```

```
hello from Go
```

Four things worth naming:

- **`package main`** — every Go file belongs to a package. The one called `main` is
  special: it is the package that produces an executable. Everything else is a library.
- **`import "fmt"`** — the standard library's formatted-I/O package. Roughly `<cstdio>`
  and `<iostream>` in one, minus the operator overloading.
- **`func main()`** — no arguments, no return value. Command-line arguments live in
  `os.Args`, and you set the exit code with `os.Exit`. There is no `int main(int argc,
  char **argv)` here.
- **The tab.** Go indents with tabs, and you don't get an opinion. More on that below.

Two ways to run it:

```bash
go run hello.go      # compile to a temp dir and execute, in one step
go build hello.go    # leave an executable called ./hello next to the source
```

`go run` feels like a scripting language and isn't one — it really is compiling. On this
machine, a warm `go build` of that file takes **0.3 seconds** and produces a **2.2 MB**
binary. That size is not bloat so much as honesty: the Go runtime, garbage collector and
scheduler are all inside it. In exchange:

```
$ file hello
hello: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, statically linked

$ ldd hello
	not a dynamic executable
```

**Statically linked. No shared library dependencies at all.** Copy that file to a bare
container with nothing in it and it runs. If you have ever shipped a C++ binary and
discovered the target box had the wrong `libstdc++`, you can probably see why this single
property is most of the reason Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are all
written in Go. Deployment is `scp`.

### Refusal one: an unused variable is an error

```go
func main() {
	count := 42
	fmt.Println("hi")
}
```

```
./bad.go:6:2: declared and not used: count
```

Not a warning. The build **fails**. Every other language you have used treats this as a
lint at most — C++ has `-Wunused-variable`, which is off unless you asked for it and
which everyone ignores anyway inside a wall of template errors.

### Refusal two: an unused import is also an error

```go
import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
)
```

```
./bad2.go:5:2: "os" imported and not used
```

This one gets people genuinely angry, because it fires constantly while you are still
*writing* the code — you comment out four lines to test something and the program stops
compiling for reasons unrelated to what you were doing.

The reasoning is that both of these are almost always the fingerprint of a real bug:
you declared a variable meaning to use it and then used a different one; you imported a
package for a call you deleted. Catching them costs a rebuild; missing them costs an
afternoon. The unused import has a second motive too — an import is a dependency, and
dependencies you don't use still cost compile time for everyone who builds your package.

The escape hatches exist, and they are deliberately ugly enough that you won't leave them
in by accident:

```go
_ = count   // "yes, I know, I am not using this yet"
```

```go
import _ "net/http/pprof"   // import ONLY for its side effects (its init function)
```

That second one is not a hack — it is the standard way to register something. Importing
`net/http/pprof` for its side effect is how you bolt a live profiler onto a running Go
server, which is a genuinely great trick you will meet again.

### Refusal three: you don't get to have opinions about formatting

```bash
gofmt -d ugly.go     # show what it would change
gofmt -w ugly.go     # rewrite the file in place
```

```diff
 package main
+
 import "fmt"
-func main(){
-x:=1
-fmt.Println( x )
+
+func main() {
+	x := 1
+	fmt.Println(x)
 }
```

There is one canonical format, a tool that produces it, and no configuration. Tabs, not
spaces. Braces where `gofmt` puts them, not where you like them. Every Go codebase on
earth looks the same, and the entire category of pull-request argument about brace style
simply does not exist. After a decade of `.clang-format` files that differ per project,
this is a bigger quality-of-life win than it sounds.

> [!NOTE]
> **The origin story, and the more interesting truth behind it.** Go is usually said to
> have been conceived while three engineers — Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson
> (yes, *that* Ken Thompson, of Unix and B) — waited 45 minutes for a C++ binary at Google
> to compile, in September 2007. Pike himself calls this "the origin myth for Go": the
> 45-minute build was real, and so was the frustration, but the tidy anecdote is tidier
> than what happened. Which is a useful thing to know in its own right, because the
> *frustration* is what the language is actually built out of. Nearly every refusal above
> is downstream of "how long does the build take, and how much does the reader have to
> know".

### Worth knowing: the rule everyone calls a language rule is technically optional

The Go specification ships with your Go installation — `/usr/local/go/doc/go_spec.html`
on a typical Linux setup. Search it for the unused-variable rule and here is the exact
wording:

> Implementation restriction: A compiler may make it illegal to declare a variable inside
> a function body if the variable is never used.

**May.** The language does not require it; it *permits* a compiler to. The `gc` compiler
you are using exercises that permission, so in practice it is a rule — but it is a rule
the toolchain chose, not one the language demands, which is a distinction almost nobody
who complains about it knows. Reading the actual spec of a language you are learning is
an unreasonably high-value hour, and Go's is short enough to make that realistic.

quiz.prompt: `go run hello.go` executes your program immediately, the way `python script.py` does. What is it actually doing underneath, and how does that differ from an interpreter?

options.text: Compiling to a real machine-code binary in a temporary directory and then executing it — the convenience is a wrapper, not interpretation
options.why: Go is compiled, always. `go run` just hides the build step and throws the binary away afterwards. This is why it feels like scripting and still produces native-speed code, and why a warm build of a small file takes about a third of a second rather than the minutes a comparable C++ translation unit can.

options.text: It compiles to bytecode that the Go runtime executes
options.why: The Go runtime is real — it carries the scheduler and garbage collector — but it is linked *into* your native binary, not a bytecode interpreter running above it.

options.text: It interprets the source directly, like CPython does with bytecode
options.why: There is no Go interpreter in the standard toolchain. If it were interpreting, `go build` could not produce a standalone executable that runs on a machine with no Go installed — and it does exactly that.

options.text: It JIT-compiles the hot paths while running, like the JVM
options.why: No JIT. Everything is compiled ahead of time, before a single line runs. Go deliberately has no VM to warm up, which is why a Go process reaches full speed on its first request rather than its thousandth.

quiz.prompt: Your Go build fails with `"os" imported and not used`. Give two separate reasons the language designers made this an error rather than a warning.

options.text: It prevents name collisions between packages
options.why: Collisions are handled separately, by qualifying every use with the package name and by letting you rename an import. An unused import cannot collide with anything precisely because nothing refers to it.

options.text: Go has no linker, so every import must be reachable
options.why: Go very much has a linker, and it does dead-code elimination. The rule is a front-end policy, enforced long before linking.

options.text: Unused imports would make the binary larger, and Go binaries are already large
options.why: Half a reason at best. The linker drops code nothing reaches, so an unused import costs little in the final binary — the cost is in *compiling* it, which the linker cannot undo.

options.text: An unused import is usually the fingerprint of a real bug, and every import is a dependency that costs compile time for everyone who builds the package
options.why: Two independent motives, which is why the rule survived the complaints. The first is correctness — you imported it for a call you have since deleted or misspelled. The second is the one people forget: Go's compile speed is a design goal, not a happy accident, and unused dependencies are a tax on it.

quiz.prompt: A Go "hello world" binary is around 2 MB where the C equivalent is a few kilobytes. What is in there, and what do you get in exchange for the size?

options.text: The source code, embedded so the runtime can recompile hot paths
options.why: Nothing recompiles at runtime; there is no JIT. The source is not shipped inside the binary.

options.text: Debug symbols, which is why release builds are small
options.why: Symbols are part of it and you can strip them with `-ldflags="-s -w"`, but that saves a fraction. The bulk is runtime and library code that is genuinely being shipped.

options.text: The Go runtime — scheduler, garbage collector, type information — all statically linked, so the binary has no shared-library dependencies at all
options.why: `ldd` on it reports "not a dynamic executable". That property is why Go took over container tooling: you can copy the binary into an empty image and it runs, with no libc version to match and no runtime to install. Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform are all downstream of this trade.

options.text: A copy of the standard library in full, since Go cannot tell which parts you use
options.why: The linker does eliminate unreached code — a hello world does not carry `net/http`. What it cannot eliminate is the runtime itself, which every Go program needs from its first instruction.

quiz.prompt: You are mid-debug, you commented out the only line using a variable, and Go now refuses to compile. What is the one-line escape hatch, and why is it written to be slightly ugly?

options.text: Declaring it with `var` instead of `:=`
options.why: The rule is about use, not about which declaration syntax produced it. A `var` declared inside a function and never used fails exactly the same way.

options.text: Building with a flag such as `go build -allow-unused`
options.why: No such flag exists, and its absence is intentional: a project-wide switch would be turned on once and never turned off.

options.text: A `//go:nolint` comment above the declaration
options.why: That family of directives is for third-party linters, not the compiler. No comment turns off a compile error in Go — the toolchain deliberately offers no pragma for this.

options.text: Assign it to the blank identifier — `_ = count` — and the ugliness is the point, so it does not survive code review by accident
options.why: `_` is Go's write-only variable: assignments to it are discarded and it counts as a use. It is deliberately conspicuous, because a silent way to disable the check would defeat the check. The same identifier does duty everywhere you want to ignore something, including discarding one of several return values.

quiz.prompt: What does `import _ "net/http/pprof"` do, given that the blank identifier means you never refer to the package by name?

options.text: Imports every exported name into the current namespace, like a wildcard
options.why: That is `import . "pkg"`, the dot import, which is discouraged precisely because it makes it impossible to see where a name came from. The blank identifier is the opposite: no names at all.

options.text: Imports it purely for its side effects — its init function runs, registering profiling handlers on the default HTTP mux
options.why: A package's `init` runs on import whether or not you call anything in it, and the blank import says "I want exactly that and nothing else". For pprof it means a running server gains live CPU, heap and goroutine profiling endpoints for one line of code. Database drivers register themselves the same way.

options.text: Imports it lazily, so it is only loaded if something needs it at runtime
options.why: There is no lazy import in Go — linking happens at build time and init runs at startup. The blank import changes what you may *name*, not when it loads.

options.text: Silences the unused-import error while leaving the package genuinely unused
options.why: It does silence the error, but "genuinely unused" is wrong and that is the whole point: the package is doing work through its init function. Using a blank import on a package with no side effects accomplishes nothing.

task.markdown:
Get Go on your machine and make the compiler shout at you on purpose. The refusals are
the lesson; meeting them deliberately now is much better than meeting them at 11pm.

Install Go from your package manager or from the official downloads — `go version` should
print something like `go version go1.24.7 linux/amd64`.

1. Write and run the hello program with `go run`.
2. Build it with `go build`, then check the result: how big is the binary, and what does
   `file` say about it? On Linux, what does `ldd` say?
3. Add a variable you never use. Record the exact error message.
4. Add an import you never use. Record that error too.
5. Make both errors go away *without* deleting the lines — use `_ =` for the variable and
   the blank import for the package.
6. Deliberately mangle the formatting — no spaces around operators, brace on its own
   line, spaces instead of tabs — then run `gofmt -d` on it and read the diff before
   running `gofmt -w`.

Keep every error message you saw in the file as a comment beside the line that caused it.
checklist: `go version` printed, and hello world ran under `go run`
binary built, its size and `file`/`ldd` output recorded
`declared and not used` triggered on purpose, message recorded
`imported and not used` triggered on purpose, message recorded
both silenced with `_` rather than by deleting the lines
`gofmt -d` diff read before `gofmt -w` was run

days.title: Zero values, and the walrus that bites
days.teaser: Why the same three lines can leave your variable untouched and never warn you
days.teachBack: Explain what shadowing is in Go, using the `data, err := reload()` shape inside an `if` block. Say precisely which variables are new, what happens to the outer ones, and why `go vet` was deliberately left unable to warn about it.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Yesterday was the toolchain. Today is the part of Go you will type a thousand times:
declaring things. It is a small topic with two genuinely sharp edges in it.

### There is no uninitialised memory

```go
var i int
var s string
var p *int
fmt.Printf("int=%d string=%q ptr=%v\n", i, s, p)
```

```
int=0 string="" ptr=<nil>
```

Every type in Go has a **zero value**, and every declaration without an initialiser gets
it. Numbers are `0`, strings are `""`, booleans are `false`, pointers and slices and maps
and interfaces are `nil`. Structs are a struct of zero values, all the way down:

```
struct={X:0 Y:0}
slice=[] len=0
```

If you have written C or C++, stop and appreciate how much this deletes. `int i;` at
block scope in C is *indeterminate* — reading it is undefined behaviour, and undefined
behaviour is not "you get a garbage number", it is "the optimiser may now assume this
line is unreachable and delete your bounds check". A decade of security advisories lives
in that gap. Go closes it by fiat: the value is always defined, and it always costs one
memory write you can't opt out of.

The design payoff is that zero values are chosen to be *useful*, not merely defined. A
`nil` slice has length 0 and you can `append` to it. A `sync.Mutex`'s zero value is an
unlocked mutex, so `var mu sync.Mutex` is ready to use with no constructor. Go has no
constructors at all, and this is why it can get away with that.

### Two ways to declare, and one of them is only for inside functions

```go
var count int = 42   // explicit type and value
var count = 42       // type inferred; still a var
count := 42          // short declaration — same thing, function bodies only
```

The `:=` form is universally nicknamed the walrus, and it is what you will write almost
everywhere. It declares *and* assigns, and infers the type. At package level you must use
`var`, because `:=` needs a function body to live in.

### The sharp edge: `:=` always declares something new

```go
count := 1
if true {
	count := 2 // a NEW variable that shadows the outer one
	_ = count
}
fmt.Println("outer count is", count)
```

```
outer count is 1
```

The inner `count` is a different variable that happens to share a name, and it dies at
the closing brace. The outer one was never touched. This is **shadowing**, it compiles
without a murmur, and it is the single most common way a Go program silently does nothing.

The version that actually bites in real code looks like this, because it does not even
have an obvious inner scope:

```go
data, err := load()
if err != nil { return err }

if needsRefresh {
	data, err := reload()      // both are new; the outer data is unchanged
	if err != nil { return err }
	_ = data
}
use(data)                      // still the old data. No warning, no error.
```

Note what saves you *sometimes*: if at least one variable on the left is new, `:=` will
**assign** to the existing ones rather than redeclare them — but only within the same
scope. Cross a brace and everything is new again. The fix is to use plain `=` when you
mean assignment, and to declare `err` once at the top of the function.

`go vet` does not catch this. Run `go tool vet help` and read the list of registered
analyzers — there are thirty-odd, checking everything from `Printf` argument types to
locks copied by value, and `shadow` is not among them. It exists, as a separate analyzer
you can attach with `go vet -vettool=...`, and it is kept out of the default set because
on idiomatic Go it fires constantly on shadowing that is entirely intentional. So this
one is on you, and knowing the shape of it is most of the defence.

### No implicit numeric conversions. None.

```go
var a int = 3
var b int64 = 4
fmt.Println(a + b)
```

```
./conv.go:8:14: invalid operation: a + b (mismatched types int and int64)
```

Even though `int` is 64 bits on this machine, `int` and `int64` are **different types**
and Go will not quietly bridge them. You write `a + int(b)` and mean it.

If you have fought C's integer promotions — where comparing a signed `int` with an
unsigned `size_t` silently converts one of them and your `i >= 0` loop guard becomes
permanently true — you will recognise what is being prevented here. C's conversion rules
are a lattice you have to memorise; Go's rule is one sentence: *there aren't any*. The
cost is `int(...)` noise in arithmetic that mixes widths. The benefit is that the noise
is exactly where the danger is.

### Worth knowing: constants are not values, and they are arbitrarily precise

```go order
const big = 1 << 62
const huge = big * 4
fmt.Println(float64(huge) / 1e18)
```

An untyped constant in Go is not stored in any machine type until it is used in a place
that needs one. It lives at arbitrary precision during compilation, so `huge` above is
`2^64` — a value that fits in no Go integer type at all — and only becomes a problem if
you try to put it in one. This is why `math.MaxUint64` can be written as a plain constant,
and why `const Pi = 3.14159265358979323846264338327950288419716939937510582097494459` is
legal and keeps every digit that the type you eventually assign it to can hold.

```
18.446744073709553
```

That is 2^64 divided by 10^18 — a constant larger than `uint64` can hold, computed
exactly and only then converted. Try to store it somewhere too small and the failure is
at compile time, not runtime:

```
./over.go:8:16: cannot use big (untyped int constant 4611686018427387904) as int32 value
in variable declaration (overflows)
```

Note that the compiler tells you the *value* it computed. That is an error message you
can only get from a language that does its constant arithmetic before choosing a type.

quiz.prompt: In Go, what is the value of `var count int` before you assign anything to it, and how does that differ from `int count;` inside a function in C?

options.text: Exactly 0, guaranteed — where C leaves it indeterminate, and reading it is undefined behaviour rather than merely a garbage number
options.why: Every Go type has a zero value and every declaration without an initialiser gets it. The C difference is sharper than "you get junk": undefined behaviour licenses the optimiser to assume the read never happens, which is how it deletes surrounding checks. Go pays one unavoidable memory write to remove the entire category.

options.text: It is an error to declare a variable without initialising it
options.why: `var count int` is perfectly legal and extremely common. The error Go does raise is for a variable you never *use*, which is a different rule.

options.text: Undefined, exactly as in C — Go simply zeroes it in practice on most platforms
options.why: It is specified, not incidental. The zero value is part of the language, so you may rely on it across every compiler and platform — which is precisely what you may not do in C.

options.text: Whatever was previously on the stack, which is why Go encourages `:=`
options.why: That describes C. In Go the memory is zeroed regardless of what was there before, and `:=` is preferred for brevity, not safety.

quiz.prompt: Name two zero values deliberately chosen so the zero value is immediately usable, and say what you can do with them without initialising anything.

options.text: A nil map, which can be written to; and a nil pointer, which can be dereferenced safely
options.why: Both halves are wrong, and dangerously so. Writing to a nil map panics — maps are the notable exception to the useful-zero-value rule and must be made with `make`. Dereferencing a nil pointer panics too.

options.text: An int, which is 0; and a string, which is empty
options.why: True but trivial — those are just the arithmetic identities, not cases where a designer chose the representation so that no initialisation step is needed. The interesting examples are the composite types.

options.text: A nil channel, which can be sent on; and a nil interface, on which methods can be called
options.why: A send on a nil channel blocks forever, and calling a method on a nil interface panics. Both are the opposite of usable — though the blocking nil channel is genuinely exploited in some select-loop idioms.

options.text: A nil slice, which has length 0 and can be appended to; and a `sync.Mutex`, whose zero value is an unlocked mutex ready to lock
options.why: This is the "make the zero value useful" design rule, and it is why Go can get away with having no constructors at all. `var s []int` then `append(s, 1)` works; `var mu sync.Mutex` then `mu.Lock()` works. A type whose zero value is broken is considered a design smell in Go.

quiz.prompt: You write `count := 2` inside an `if` block when `count` already exists outside it. What happens to the outer variable, and what is this mistake called?

options.text: The outer variable is assigned 2, since `:=` falls back to assignment
options.why: There is a fallback, but it does not cross scopes: within *one* scope, `:=` will assign to existing variables as long as at least one name on the left is new. Cross a brace and every name is new again.

options.text: The outer variable becomes nil until the block exits
options.why: Nothing happens to the outer variable at all, and `nil` is not a value an `int` can hold.

options.text: It fails to compile, because the name is already taken in an enclosing scope
options.why: Shadowing is legal and often deliberate — that is exactly why the compiler stays quiet and why the shadow analyzer is kept out of the default `go vet` suite.

options.text: Nothing — a new variable is created that hides the outer one until the closing brace, which is shadowing
options.why: `:=` always declares. The outer variable is untouched, the inner one dies at the brace, and nothing warns you. It is the most common way a Go program silently does nothing, and it is nastiest in the `data, err := reload()` shape inside an `if`, where there is no obviously suspicious inner scope to look at.

quiz.prompt: Go refuses to compile `a + b` where `a` is `int` and `b` is `int64`, even on a machine where both are 64 bits wide. Why, and what class of C bug does it prevent?

options.text: They are distinct types and Go performs no implicit numeric conversion at all — which removes C's promotion rules, where a signed/unsigned comparison silently converts one side
options.why: Identical width does not mean identical type. The C bug being designed out is the signed-versus-unsigned comparison: compare an `int` loop counter with a `size_t` and the int is converted to unsigned, making `i >= 0` permanently true. C's conversion rules are a lattice you memorise; Go's rule is that there are none, and the `int(b)` you must write sits exactly where the danger was.

options.text: `int` is 32 bits on some platforms, so the addition could overflow
options.why: Go's `int` is platform-dependent in size, but that is not the reason — the compiler rejects this even where it can prove both are 64 bits. The rule is about type identity, not representable range.

options.text: Because `+` is not defined for `int64`, only for `int`
options.why: `+` works fine on `int64`; `b + b` compiles. What fails is mixing two different types in one operation.

options.text: Go requires explicit conversion only when precision could be lost
options.why: There is no such exemption. Widening conversions that could not possibly lose anything still have to be written out, which is the point: one rule, no exceptions to remember.

quiz.prompt: Why can `const huge = (1 << 62) * 4` compile in Go when no Go integer type can hold that value?

options.text: It is stored as a float64, which has the range even if it loses precision
options.why: Constants are not secretly floats; integer constants stay exact integers. If they were float64 the compiler could not report the precise value 18446744073709551616 in its overflow message.

options.text: The compiler promotes it to `uint64`, which is large enough
options.why: `uint64`'s maximum is 18446744073709551615, one less than this value — so even the widest integer type does not hold it, and that is exactly what makes the example worth showing.

options.text: It silently wraps around, as unsigned arithmetic does at runtime
options.why: No wrapping happens — that is the behaviour being avoided. Ask for it in a type too small and you get a compile error, not a wrapped value.

options.text: Untyped constants are evaluated at arbitrary precision during compilation and only take a machine type when used somewhere that needs one
options.why: The constant exists as an exact mathematical value until context forces a type on it, so `float64(huge)` is fine while `var x int64 = huge` fails at compile time with the computed value quoted back at you. It is also why a Pi constant can carry more digits than any type holds and still be correct for whichever type eventually receives it.

Prove the zero values and then get shadowed on purpose, so that the day you meet it in
real code you recognise the shape.

1. Declare one variable of each of these with `var` and no initialiser: an `int`, a
   `float64`, a `string`, a `bool`, a pointer, a slice, and a struct with two fields.
   Print them all with `%v` and the string with `%q` so you can see it is empty rather
   than absent.
2. Append to the `nil` slice without initialising it first, and print the result. It
   should work; be clear with yourself about why.
3. Write the shadowing trap: a variable set outside a block, reassigned with `:=` inside
   it, printed after. Then fix it so the outer variable really changes, and record what
   you changed.
4. Try to add an `int` to an `int64`. Record the exact error, then make it compile.
5. Declare a constant larger than `int64` can hold, use it in a `float64` expression, and
   then deliberately try to assign it to an `int32` and record that error too.

days.title: Slices are not arrays
days.teaser: The append that silently rewrites a slice you never passed in
days.teachBack: A slice header has three fields. Use them to explain why `append` to a two-element sub-slice of a five-element slice can overwrite the original's data without allocating — and what the third index in `full[:2:2]` changes about that.
days.theoryMarkdown:
This is the day Go stops feeling obvious. Slices are the type you will use constantly,
they look like a dynamic array from any other language, and they have one behaviour that
will eventually cost you an afternoon. Better to spend twenty minutes on it now.

### An array is a value. A slice is a view.

Go has both, and they are different types with different behaviour.

```go order
a := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
b := a
b[0] = 99
fmt.Println("array a:", a, " b:", b)
```

```
array a: [1 2 3]  b: [99 2 3]
```

`[3]int` is an **array**: the length is part of the type, and assigning one **copies all
the elements**. `[3]int` and `[4]int` are as unrelated as `int` and `string`.

Now the same thing with a slice:

```go order
s := []int{1, 2, 3}
t := s
t[0] = 99
fmt.Println("slice s:", s, " t:", t)
```

```
slice s: [99 2 3]  t: [99 2 3]
```

Both changed. `[]int` — no number in the brackets — is a **slice**, and a slice is a
small three-word header:

```
┌──────────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ ptr to array │  len   │  cap   │
└──────────────┴────────┴────────┘
```

Copying a slice copies the *header*, not the elements. Both headers point at the same
backing array. If you know C++, a slice is close to a `std::span` — except that it also
owns its backing array in the eyes of the garbage collector, and it can grow.

**Almost every Go program uses slices and almost never uses arrays directly.** Arrays
mostly appear as the thing a slice points at, and as fixed-size buffers like `[32]byte`
for a hash.

### `len` is what's there, `cap` is what fits

```go order
var s []int
s = append(s, 1)
fmt.Printf("len=%d cap=%d\n", len(s), cap(s))
```

`append` writes into spare capacity if there is any. When there isn't, it allocates a
bigger array, copies everything across, and returns a slice pointing at the new one.
Watch it happen:

```
len= 1 cap= 1  <- grew
len= 2 cap= 2  <- grew
len= 3 cap= 4  <- grew
len= 5 cap= 8  <- grew
len= 9 cap=16  <- grew
```

Doubling, and the same amortised-constant-time argument as `std::vector`. This is also
why `append` **returns** the slice and you must write `s = append(s, x)`: when it
reallocates, your old header is pointing at the abandoned array. Forgetting the
assignment is a beginner error, and one of the few places Go's strictness saves you for
free:

```
./noassign.go:7:2: append(s, 2) (value of type []int) is not used
```

Yesterday's rule about unused things, doing an honest day's work.

If you know roughly how many elements you'll have, say so and skip the copying:

```go
s := make([]int, 0, 1000)   // len 0, cap 1000
```

### The trap

Here is the one to actually remember. A sub-slice shares the original's backing array,
and it inherits capacity all the way to the end of it:

```go order
full := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
head := full[:2]
fmt.Printf("head=%v len=%d cap=%d\n", head, len(head), cap(head))
head = append(head, 99)
fmt.Println("full is now:", full)
```

```
head=[1 2] len=2 cap=5
full is now: [1 2 99 4 5]
```

Read that twice. `head` looks like a two-element slice, but its capacity is **5** — it can
see all the way to the end of `full`'s array. So `append` finds spare room, does not
allocate, and writes 99 straight over `full[2]`. A function that took `head` as a
parameter and appended to it just silently corrupted a slice it was never given.

The fix is a **three-index slice**, which sets the capacity explicitly:

```go order
full := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
head := full[:2:2]
fmt.Printf("head=%v len=%d cap=%d\n", head, len(head), cap(head))
head = append(head, 99)
fmt.Println("full is now:", full)
```

```
head=[1 2] len=2 cap=2
full is now: [1 2 3 4 5]
```

`full[:2:2]` means low 0, high 2, **max 2** — capacity 2. Now `append` has no room, must
allocate, and `full` is untouched. When you hand a sub-slice to code you don't control,
this is how you do it safely.

There is a C++ echo here worth noticing. Appending to a `std::vector` invalidates
iterators and pointers into it, and everyone learns that rule. Go's version is stranger:
`append` never invalidates anything — the old array stays alive as long as something
points at it, because the garbage collector says so — but it may or may not *share* with
what you had before, and which one you get depends on capacity. C++ makes the old view
invalid; Go makes it valid and possibly aliased, which is quieter and therefore worse to
debug.

### Worth knowing: a giant array can be kept alive by a tiny slice

Because a slice holds a pointer into a backing array, the whole array stays reachable
even if your slice covers three bytes of it:

```go
data, _ := os.ReadFile("500mb.log")   // 500 MB
firstLine := data[:60]                // still pins all 500 MB
```

Hold `firstLine` in a cache and you have leaked half a gigabyte — a leak in a garbage
collected language, which is not supposed to be a thing you can do. The standard fix is
to copy what you actually want out:

```go
firstLine := append([]byte(nil), data[:60]...)   // fresh array, 60 bytes
```

Since Go 1.21 the standard library ships `slices.Clone` for exactly this, and you can
watch the pin let go — clone a 5-byte head of a 41-byte array and the copy reports
`cap=8` instead of `cap=41`, because it is a genuinely new array. If you ever
wondered how a Go service leaks memory without a single missing `free`, this is the
most common answer, along with goroutines that never exit — which is Day 6's problem.

quiz.prompt: `a := [3]int{1,2,3}; b := a; b[0] = 99`. What is `a[0]` afterwards, and what would have happened if both had been slices instead?

options.text: `a[0]` is still 1, because assigning an array copies every element — with slices both would read 99, because assigning a slice copies only the header
options.why: This is the whole distinction. `[3]int` is a value type whose length is part of the type, so assignment is a full copy. `[]int` is a three-word header — pointer, length, capacity — and copying it leaves two headers pointing at one backing array. Nearly every Go surprise involving slices comes back to this.

options.text: `a[0]` is 99 in both cases; Go assigns by reference like Java or Python
options.why: Go has no reference assignment. Everything is copied — the question is only ever *what* gets copied, and for a slice that is the header rather than the elements.

options.text: `a[0]` is 1 in both cases, since Go copies on assignment everywhere
options.why: Right about arrays, wrong about slices. The copy is real for both, but copying a slice's header duplicates a pointer, and both copies then address the same elements.

options.text: It depends on whether the array escapes to the heap
options.why: Escape analysis decides *where* a value lives, never what assignment means. Copy semantics are the same on the stack and the heap.

quiz.prompt: What are the three fields of a Go slice header, and which of them does copying a slice copy?

options.text: A pointer to a backing array, a length and a capacity — and copying duplicates all three, which duplicates the pointer rather than the elements
options.why: Three machine words. Because the pointer is duplicated rather than the array, two slices can disagree about length while addressing identical memory — which is exactly the situation the append trap exploits.

options.text: The elements, the length and the capacity; copying duplicates all the elements
options.why: That describes an array, and it is the behaviour slices exist to avoid. Passing a large slice to a function costs three words, not the data.

options.text: A pointer, a length, and a type tag; copying duplicates the pointer only
options.why: There is no type tag in a slice header — the element type is static and known at compile time. The third word is capacity, and it is the one that decides whether an append allocates.

options.text: A pointer and a length; capacity is computed from the backing array when needed
options.why: Capacity is stored, not computed — a slice has no way to ask an array how big it is, since the pointer may address the middle of one. `cap()` is a field read.

quiz.prompt: Why must you write `s = append(s, x)` in Go rather than just `append(s, x)`?

options.text: Because append may return an error alongside the slice
options.why: Append returns exactly one value, the slice. It has no error case — it panics only if allocation itself fails, which takes the process with it.

options.text: Because when there is no spare capacity, append allocates a new array and returns a slice pointing at it — your old header would still address the abandoned one
options.why: Append cannot modify your header in place; it only has a copy of it. When it grows the array, the only way to hand you the result is the return value. Discarding it is caught by the compiler — `append(s, 2) (value of type []int) is not used` — which is yesterday's unused-value rule earning its keep.

options.text: Because append is a pure function and Go forbids side effects in builtins
options.why: Append is not pure at all — when there *is* spare capacity it writes straight into the existing backing array, which is visible to every other slice sharing it. That is precisely what makes the aliasing trap possible.

options.text: Purely stylistic; `append(s, x)` works but reads badly
options.why: It does not work, and it does not compile. Even if it did, it would lose the element whenever the array had to grow.

quiz.prompt: `head := full[:2]` where `full` has five elements. What is `cap(head)`, and what does `append(head, 99)` do to `full`?

options.text: `cap(head)` is 5, and append allocates anyway because len is less than cap
options.why: Backwards: append allocates only when len *equals* cap. Room to spare is exactly the condition for writing in place.

options.text: `cap(head)` is 5, so append finds spare room and overwrites `full[2]` in place — `full` becomes [1 2 99 4 5]
options.why: A sub-slice inherits capacity all the way to the end of the backing array, so `head` can see memory it does not appear to own. No allocation happens, so the write lands in the original. A function handed `head` can corrupt data it was never shown, silently.

options.text: `cap(head)` is 2, so append allocates and `full` is unaffected
options.why: That is what `full[:2:2]` gives you — the three-index form that sets capacity explicitly. Plain `full[:2]` leaves capacity running to the end of the array, which is what makes this a trap rather than a footnote.

options.text: It panics, because appending past a sub-slice's length is out of bounds
options.why: Append never panics for this reason — extending beyond length is its entire job. Indexing past length panics; appending past it does not.

quiz.prompt: You read a 500 MB file into memory and keep a 60-byte slice of it in a cache. How much memory stays reachable, and what is the fix?

options.text: 60 bytes — the collector frees the rest of the array once nothing indexes it
options.why: There is no partial collection of an array. The allocation is the unit, and it survives entirely or not at all.

options.text: All 500 MB, and the only fix is to call `runtime.GC()` after slicing
options.why: Right about the leak, wrong about the remedy — and this is a trap worth avoiding on its own. Forcing a collection cannot free memory that is still reachable, and the slice makes it reachable. You have to break the pointer, not nudge the collector.

options.text: 60 bytes, because slicing copies in Go
options.why: Slicing never copies; that is the property that makes it cheap. Copying is the thing you have to ask for explicitly, which is what the fix does.

options.text: All 500 MB, because the slice's pointer keeps the whole backing array alive — fixed by copying the 60 bytes into a fresh slice, e.g. `slices.Clone`
options.why: The garbage collector frees arrays, not ranges. One live pointer into an array keeps every byte of it reachable, so a 60-byte view pins half a gigabyte. This is how you leak memory in a garbage-collected language with no missing free, and along with goroutines that never exit it is the most common cause of a Go service growing without explanation.

task.markdown:
Reproduce the trap. This is not a puzzle you should take on faith — it is far more

1. Make an array and a slice of the same three values. Assign each to a second variable,

2. Append to an empty slice in a loop, printing `len` and `cap` each time the capacity

capacity growth pattern recorded from a real loop
the aliasing trap reproduced, with the sub-slice's capacity recorded
the three-index fix shown protecting the original

days.title: Methods, and interfaces you never declare
days.teaser: strings.Builder has never heard of io.Writer, and satisfies it anyway
days.teachBack: In Go a type implements an interface without ever naming it. Explain who decides what an interface contains under that arrangement versus a language with an `implements` keyword, and why that inversion is what makes one-method interfaces like `io.Writer` so widely satisfied.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Go has no classes, no inheritance, no `virtual`, no constructors and no `this`. It has
structs, functions attached to types, and one of the better ideas in mainstream language
design: interfaces that types satisfy without ever mentioning them.

### A method is a function with a receiver

```go
type Counter struct {
	n int
}

func (c *Counter) Bump() {
	c.n++
}
```

The `(c *Counter)` before the name is the **receiver**. That is the whole mechanism —
there is no class body, methods live at package level next to everything else, and the
receiver is an ordinary parameter that happens to be written in front. You can define
methods on any named type you declared, not just structs:

```go
type Celsius float64

func (c Celsius) String() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%.1f°C", float64(c)) }
```

### The one decision that trips everyone: value or pointer receiver

```go
func (c Counter) BumpValue()    { c.n++ }
func (c *Counter) BumpPointer() { c.n++ }
```

```
after value receiver:   0
after pointer receiver: 1
```

`BumpValue` receives a **copy** of the Counter. It increments the copy, the copy is
discarded, and your original is untouched — and nothing warns you, because incrementing a
local is perfectly legal. `BumpPointer` receives the address and modifies the real thing.

The rule in practice: **if the method modifies the receiver, or the struct is large, use
a pointer. Then use a pointer for all its methods**, even the ones that don't need it,
because a type whose method set is half values and half pointers is a type whose
behaviour depends on how you happened to call it.

Go does hide one piece of sugar here. You never write `(&c).BumpPointer()` — if `c` is
addressable, Go inserts the `&` for you. That is why `c.BumpPointer()` compiles when `c`
is a `Counter` and not a `*Counter`. C++ makes you pick `.` or `->`; Go decided that
distinction never carried information and removed it.

### Interfaces: satisfied by accident, on purpose

```go
type Greeter interface {
	Greet() string
}

type English struct{ Name string }

func (e English) Greet() string { return "Hello, " + e.Name }
```

```go
var g Greeter = English{Name: "world"}
fmt.Println(g.Greet())
```

```
Hello, world
```

Notice what is **not** there. `English` does not say `implements Greeter`. There is no
`: public Greeter`, no `@Override`, no registration. It has a method with the right name
and signature, so it satisfies the interface. Full stop.

This is **structural typing**, and it inverts who is in charge. In C++ or Java, the
author of a class decides which interfaces it implements, and if they didn't think of
yours you are writing an adapter. In Go the *consumer* declares the interface, and every
existing type that happens to fit is instantly compatible — including types from
libraries written years before your interface existed.

Watch it happen with the standard library:

```go
var sb strings.Builder
fmt.Fprintf(&sb, "written through io.Writer: %d", 42)
```

```
written through io.Writer: 42
```

`fmt.Fprintf` takes an `io.Writer`. `strings.Builder` never mentions `io.Writer`
anywhere. It has a `Write([]byte) (int, error)` method, which is all `io.Writer` asks
for, so it fits. The same one-method interface is satisfied by files, network
connections, HTTP response writers, gzip compressors, hash functions and
`os.Stdout` — which is why "write it to a string instead of the network" is a
one-line change in Go and a refactor in most languages.

`io.Writer` is worth staring at, because it is the whole philosophy in four lines:

```go
type Writer interface {
	Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **"The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction."** That is Rob Pike, in his Go
> proverbs, and it is the opposite of the instinct most of us bring from other languages
> where interfaces accumulate methods to be "complete". In Go the most useful interfaces
> in the entire ecosystem have exactly one method: `io.Writer`, `io.Reader`, `error`,
> `fmt.Stringer`, `http.Handler`. A one-method interface is trivially satisfiable, so
> almost everything satisfies it, so it composes with everything.
>
> You will also constantly hear **"accept interfaces, return structs"** quoted alongside
> it, usually as though it were a second proverb. It isn't — it is a community idiom that
> never made the canonical list — but it falls straight out of the real one: take the
> loosest thing you can work with, hand back the most specific thing you have.

### Worth knowing: the compile-time assertion nobody shows beginners

Because nothing declares intent, nothing tells you when you *meant* to satisfy an
interface and got the signature subtly wrong — a value receiver where a pointer was
needed, `Str()` instead of `String()`. The code compiles; it just isn't a `Stringer`, and
you find out when your log line prints `{0 0}` instead of your nice format.

The idiom for this is a variable declaration that does nothing:

```go
var _ Greeter = English{}     // fails to compile if English stops satisfying Greeter
var _ Greeter = (*Spanish)(nil)  // same check, for a pointer receiver, with no allocation
```

Assign to the blank identifier, so nothing is stored and nothing is used, but the type
check still runs — and when it fails it tells you exactly which method is missing:

```
./assert.go:16:17: cannot use Broken{} (value of struct type Broken) as Greeter value in
variable declaration: Broken does not implement Greeter (missing method Greet)
``` You will find this line near the top of a great many real Go files, and
it is one of those things that looks like line noise until someone explains it once.

quiz.prompt: What is a receiver in Go, and where does it appear in a method declaration?

options.text: The interface a method belongs to, declared before the method name
options.why: Methods are attached to concrete types, never to interfaces. An interface only lists signatures; it never contains a method body or claims one.

options.text: The return type, written before the name as in C
options.why: Go puts return types after the parameter list. The parenthesised thing before the name is the receiver, and it is a syntax Go uses nowhere else.

options.text: The parameter written in parentheses before the method name — `func (c *Counter) Bump()` — making it an ordinary parameter that happens to sit in front
options.why: There is no class body to be inside. Methods are declared at package level like any function, and the receiver is what binds one to a type. Because it is just a parameter, all the normal rules about copying apply to it, which is the whole of the next question.

options.text: The implicit `this` pointer, available inside every method
options.why: Go has no implicit `this` and no implicit anything. You name the receiver yourself, and by convention give it a one- or two-letter name rather than `self` — precisely so it reads as the parameter it is.

quiz.prompt: A Go method with a value receiver increments a field of its receiver. Why does the caller's value not change, and why is there no warning?

options.text: Because the struct escaped to the heap and the method saw a stale copy
options.why: Escape analysis is unrelated. The copy is made at the call, deterministically, whether the original lives on the stack or the heap.

options.text: Value receivers are immutable, so the assignment is silently ignored
options.why: Nothing is ignored — the copy really is modified, and you can print it inside the method to watch it change. Immutability would at least be enforceable; this is worse, because the write succeeds.

options.text: The method got a copy, incremented the copy, and discarded it — and incrementing a local variable is perfectly legal, so there is nothing for the compiler to object to
options.why: A value receiver is passed by value like any parameter. The mutation is real, it just happens to something about to be thrown away. This compiles cleanly and does nothing, which is why the guidance is to pick pointer receivers for any type with mutating methods and then use pointers for *all* of that type's methods, so the behaviour never depends on which one you happen to call.

options.text: It does change, unless the struct contains a pointer field
options.why: The caller's value never changes through a value receiver. A pointer *field* would let you reach shared data through the copy, but the receiver's own fields are still a copy.

quiz.prompt: What does a Go type have to write in order to implement an interface?

options.text: Register the type with the interface at init time
options.why: Nothing is registered and there is no runtime bookkeeping to opt into. The check happens at compile time, at the point where a value is assigned to the interface.

options.text: Embed the interface in the struct, so its method set is inherited
options.why: Embedding an interface in a struct is legal but does something else entirely: it promotes the methods of whatever value you store there, and leaves you with a type that panics when that value is nil. It is not how implementing works.

options.text: An `implements` clause naming the interface
options.why: No such clause exists in Go. The nearest thing is the voluntary `var _ Iface = Type{}` assertion, which exists only so *you* find out at compile time when you break the fit.

options.text: Nothing — having methods with the right names and signatures is the whole requirement
options.why: This is structural typing, and it inverts who is in charge. In a nominal system the author of a type decides which interfaces it implements, so if they never heard of yours you write an adapter. In Go the consumer declares the interface, and every type that already fits — including ones written years earlier — is instantly compatible.

quiz.prompt: `strings.Builder` never mentions `io.Writer` anywhere, yet `fmt.Fprintf` accepts a pointer to one. Explain how, and say who defines the interface in that arrangement.

options.text: `strings.Builder` embeds `io.Writer` internally, which is why it fits
options.why: It embeds nothing of the sort. If it did, it would need something to delegate to, and the whole point is that no link between the two types exists.

options.text: It has a `Write([]byte) (int, error)` method, which is everything `io.Writer` asks for — and the interface is defined by the consumer, `io`, not by the type
options.why: `io.Writer` is one method. That is why files, sockets, HTTP response writers, gzip compressors, hashes and `os.Stdout` all satisfy it, and why redirecting output from the network to a string is a one-line change in Go. The smallness is the feature: as Rob Pike put it, the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.

options.text: The `io` package registers known writer types, and `strings.Builder` is on the list
options.why: No list exists — and if it did, your own types could never join it, which would destroy the property that makes the design worth having.

options.text: `fmt.Fprintf` uses reflection to find a suitable method at runtime
options.why: The check is entirely static, made when the argument is converted to the interface. `fmt` does use reflection for formatting the *values*, but not to decide whether something is a Writer.

quiz.prompt: What does the line `var _ Greeter = English{}` accomplish, given that it stores nothing and is never referenced?

options.text: It silences the unused-variable error for the `Greeter` type
options.why: Types are not subject to the unused rule — only variables and imports are, and only inside function bodies for variables. This line is at package level and is there purely for the type check.

options.text: It makes the compiler verify that `English` still satisfies `Greeter`, failing the build with the missing method named if the fit ever breaks
options.why: Because nothing declares intent, nothing normally tells you that you *meant* to satisfy an interface and got the signature subtly wrong — `Str()` for `String()`, or a value receiver where a pointer was needed. This line costs nothing at runtime and turns that silence into a build error naming the missing method.

options.text: It registers `English` as an implementation so the runtime can find it
options.why: There is no registry and nothing to find. Interface satisfaction is resolved statically at each assignment.

options.text: It creates a default `Greeter` used when no other value is supplied
options.why: Assigning to the blank identifier stores nothing anywhere — the value is discarded immediately. Nothing can later retrieve it.

days.title: Errors are values, and defer is your destructor
days.teaser: No exceptions anywhere in the language, and one verb that decides whether the cause survives
days.teachBack: Explain what `%w` does that `%v` does not, given that both produce identical text. Then say what that buys a caller ten frames up the stack, and what it costs the package that wrapped the error.
days.theoryMarkdown:
Go has no exceptions. None. No `try`, no `catch`, no `throw`, no stack unwinding you can
hook into. This is the single most argued-about decision in the language, and today is
about living with it — plus `defer`, the feature that fills the hole where a C++
destructor would go.

### Errors come back like any other value

```go order
f, err := os.Open("/no/such/file")
if err != nil {
	return err
}
defer f.Close()
```

Go functions can return more than one value, and the convention — enforced by nothing but
followed by everyone — is that the last one is an `error`. `nil` means it worked.

```
err: open /no/such/file: no such file or directory
```

`error` is not a special language construct. It is an ordinary one-method interface, and
you have already met its shape:

```go
type error interface {
	Error() string
}
```

That is the entire type. Anything with an `Error() string` method is an error, which
means you write your own error types the same way you write anything else.

Yes, you will type `if err != nil` a great deal. Roughly one line in twenty of real Go is
that line. People find this either honest or unbearable and there is not much middle
ground. The argument in its favour: an exception is an invisible second control-flow graph
through your program, and every call is a potential jump to somewhere you cannot see. Go
makes the unhappy path the same size on the page as the happy path, because at 3am the
unhappy path is the one you are reading. The argument against: it is a lot of typing, it
is easy to `return err` without adding context, and unlike an exception, an error is
trivially *ignorable* — `f, _ := os.Open(...)` compiles fine.

### Wrapping: keep the cause, add the context

Returning a bare `err` upward is how you end up with `no such file or directory` and no
idea which file. Wrap it with `%w`:

```go order
_, err := os.Open("/no/such/file")
wrapped := fmt.Errorf("loading config: %w", err)
fmt.Println(wrapped)
fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapped, os.ErrNotExist))
```

```
loading config: open /no/such/file: no such file or directory
true
```

`%w` is `%v` plus a hidden link back to the original error. That link is what
`errors.Is` follows — so a caller ten frames up can still ask "was this ultimately a
file-not-found?" and get `true`, without string matching and without caring how many
layers added context on the way. `errors.As` does the same for extracting a specific
error *type*.

Swap the verb and watch the link vanish:

```
with %w: true
with %v: false
```

Same message text either way — only the machine-readable link differs. Use `%w` when the
caller might reasonably want to inspect the cause; use plain `%v` when you are
deliberately hiding the internals. Wrapping everything makes your internal error
types part of your public API, which is a real cost.

### defer: run this on the way out, whatever happens

```go
defer fmt.Println("third")
defer fmt.Println("second")
defer fmt.Println("first")
fmt.Println("body")
```

```
body
first
second
third
```

Deferred calls run when the surrounding **function** returns — not at the end of the
block, which is a genuine difference from a C++ destructor and the source of the classic
"I deferred `f.Close()` inside a loop and ran out of file descriptors" bug. They run in
**LIFO** order, which is exactly right: the thing you acquired last is the thing you
release first.

This is Go's answer to RAII, and it is a worse answer in one specific way and a better one
in another. Worse: it is opt-in and manual, so forgetting `defer f.Close()` leaks, where a
C++ destructor could not be forgotten. Better: it is *visible at the call site*. You can
see the cleanup on the line after the acquisition, rather than having to know what some
type's destructor does.

Crucially, deferred calls still run when the function panics, which is what makes them
trustworthy for unlocking mutexes:

```go
mu.Lock()
defer mu.Unlock()
```

### The defer gotcha: arguments evaluate now, the call happens later

```go order
i := 1
defer fmt.Println("deferred saw i =", i)
i = 99
fmt.Println("at the end i =", i)
```

```
at the end i = 99
deferred saw i = 1
```

The arguments were evaluated the moment the `defer` statement ran; only the *call* was
postponed. If you want the late value, defer a closure instead — `defer func() {
fmt.Println(i) }()` — which captures the variable rather than its value.

### panic exists, and is not for errors

`panic` unwinds the stack running deferred functions, and `recover` inside a deferred
function stops it. It looks like exceptions and is not meant to be used like them: panic
is for genuinely unrecoverable programmer error — index out of range, nil dereference, an
invariant you thought was impossible. A library that panics on a bad input is considered
badly behaved; it should return an error. The main legitimate use of `recover` is at the
top of a server's request handler, so one broken request doesn't take down the process.

quiz.prompt: What is the `error` type in Go, exactly — what makes a value an error?

options.text: A special type recognised by the compiler, which enforces that it is checked
options.why: The compiler enforces nothing here — `f, _ := os.Open(...)` compiles happily. That ignorability is the strongest argument *against* Go's design, and it is worth knowing it is real rather than assuming the compiler has your back.

options.text: An ordinary one-method interface: anything with an `Error() string` method is an error, with no special language support involved
options.why: The whole declaration is two lines in `builtin.go`. Because it is a plain interface, your own error types are written the way you write anything else, and `nil` — the zero value of an interface — is the natural way to say "no error". There is no exception machinery anywhere in the language for it to hook into.

options.text: A built-in struct the runtime creates when something fails
options.why: Nothing is created for you and there is no built-in struct. Errors are ordinary values that ordinary code constructs and returns, which is exactly the property that lets you compare them, wrap them and store them.

options.text: An alias for `string`, which is why errors print directly
options.why: It is an interface, not a string. Errors print nicely because `fmt` calls the `Error()` method, the same way it calls `String()` on a `fmt.Stringer`.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between wrapping an error with `%w` and formatting it with `%v`, and what does the difference make possible for a caller?

options.text: `%w` is for warnings and `%v` for values; both flatten the cause
options.why: There is no warning concept in the `fmt` verbs. `%w` stands for wrap, and it is the only verb that preserves the chain.

options.text: They are identical; `%w` is just the newer spelling
options.why: They produce identical *text*, which is what makes this trap easy to fall into, but `errors.Is` returns true through one and false through the other.

options.text: `%w` keeps a machine-readable link to the original, so `errors.Is` and `errors.As` can still find the cause however many layers were added
options.why: The printed text is identical either way; only the link differs. With `%w` a caller ten frames up can ask `errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)` and get true without string matching. With `%v` the same check returns false, because the cause was flattened into text. The cost of `%w` is that your internal error types become part of your public API.

options.text: `%w` prints the full stack trace, where `%v` prints only the message
options.why: Neither verb captures a stack trace — Go errors carry no stack by default, which is a common complaint and the reason third-party error packages exist. `%w` adds a link to another error, not a trace.

quiz.prompt: When exactly does a deferred call run in Go, and in what order relative to other defers in the same function?

options.text: When the surrounding function returns — including when it panics — and in LIFO order, last deferred first
options.why: Function scope, not block scope, which is the difference from a C++ destructor and the cause of the classic bug where `defer f.Close()` inside a loop holds every file open until the whole function ends. LIFO is the right order because the thing acquired last should be released first, and running on panic is what makes `defer mu.Unlock()` trustworthy.

options.text: At the end of the enclosing block, in LIFO order, like a C++ destructor
options.why: The LIFO half is right and the scope half is wrong, which is the most expensive way to be half right — it is precisely the assumption that produces the file-descriptor leak in a loop.

options.text: When the function returns, in the order the defers were written
options.why: The timing is right but the order is reversed. FIFO would release things in the order they were acquired, which would tear down a resource before whatever depends on it.

options.text: Only on a normal return; a panic skips deferred calls and unwinds directly
options.why: Backwards, and dangerously — deferred calls are exactly what a panic runs as it unwinds. If they were skipped, `defer mu.Unlock()` would leave a mutex locked forever, and `recover` could not exist, since it only works inside a deferred function.

quiz.prompt: `i := 1; defer fmt.Println(i); i = 99`. What does the deferred line print when the function returns, and why?

options.text: It depends on whether `i` escapes to the heap
options.why: Escape analysis changes where a value is stored, never when arguments are evaluated. The rule is the same in both cases.

options.text: 1 — the arguments were evaluated when the `defer` statement ran, and only the call itself was postponed
options.why: `defer` captures the argument values immediately; it is the invocation that waits. This bites hardest when deferring something like `f.Close()` on a variable you later reassign. When you want the value as of return time, defer a closure instead — `defer func(){ fmt.Println(i) }()` — which captures the variable rather than its value.

options.text: 99 — deferred calls read the current value at the moment they run
options.why: That is what the closure form does, and assuming it is the default is the gotcha. A plain `defer f(x)` freezes `x` at the point of the defer statement.

options.text: Nothing — the reassignment cancels the pending defer
options.why: Nothing cancels a defer once it has been scheduled; short of the process dying, the call will happen.

quiz.prompt: When is `panic` the right choice in Go rather than returning an error, and where is `recover` legitimately used?

options.text: Whenever an error would be tedious to thread upward — panic is Go's exception mechanism
options.why: It resembles one and is deliberately not used as one. Treating panic as exceptions gives you an invisible second control-flow path, which is the exact thing Go's error design exists to avoid.

options.text: Never — `panic` is a legacy feature and `recover` should not be used
options.why: Too strong. The runtime itself panics on nil dereference and out-of-range indexing, and boundary recovery in servers is standard practice — `net/http` does it for every handler it runs.

options.text: For any error a caller cannot fix, so it reaches `main` reliably
options.why: Errors a caller cannot fix are still returned; the caller decides whether to log, retry or exit. Panicking takes that decision away from every caller above you.

options.text: For genuinely unrecoverable programmer error — a broken invariant — while `recover` belongs at a boundary such as a server's request handler, so one bad request cannot kill the process
options.why: Panic is for "this cannot happen and if it did the program is already wrong", not for expected failure. A library that panics on bad input is considered badly behaved and should return an error. `recover` only works inside a deferred function, and its honest use is containment at a boundary rather than general-purpose exception handling.
