days.title: Goroutines and channels
days.teaser: 100,000 of them on four OS threads, and a runtime that tells you when they all fall asleep
days.teachBack: The runtime reports "all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!" only when every goroutine is blocked. Explain what that check can and cannot see, and why the case it misses is the one that actually shows up in production.
days.theoryMarkdown:
This is the day Go earns its reputation. Concurrency is not a library here — it is
syntax, it is cheap enough to be boring, and the runtime will tell you when you have
deadlocked.

### `go` in front of a call, and that's it

```go order
done := make(chan string)
go func() {
	done <- "worker finished"
}()
fmt.Println(<-done)
```

```
worker finished
```

`go f()` runs `f` concurrently and returns immediately. The thing that starts is a
**goroutine**, and it is not an OS thread. The Go runtime multiplexes many goroutines
onto a small pool of real threads — an **M:N scheduler** — so the cost of starting one is
an allocation, not a system call.

How cheap, concretely? Start a hundred thousand of them and ask the runtime what it is
holding:

```
goroutines: 100001
total stack in use: 200352 KB, per goroutine: ~2051 bytes
OS threads in use: 4
```

**About 2 KB each**, one hundred thousand of them alive at once, running on four OS
threads. A pthread's default stack is 8 MB of reserved address space — four thousand
times more — which is why C and C++ servers grew thread pools, work queues, and eventually
`epoll` loops with hand-rolled state machines. Go's answer is "just start a goroutine per
connection", and at these numbers that is a real answer rather than a naive one.

The stacks start small and **grow**: the runtime allocates 2 KB, and when a function
would overflow it, it allocates a bigger stack, copies the frames across and fixes up the
pointers. You cannot do that in C, where a pointer to a local must stay valid at a fixed
address — which is exactly why C stacks must be reserved large and up front.

### Channels: a typed pipe with a lock built in

```go
ch := make(chan int)      // unbuffered
ch := make(chan int, 10)  // buffered, capacity 10
ch <- 42                  // send
v := <-ch                 // receive
close(ch)                 // no more sends
```

An **unbuffered** channel is a rendezvous: the sender blocks until a receiver is ready,
and vice versa. That blocking is a synchronisation primitive — you get "handoff happened"
for free, without a mutex or a condition variable. A **buffered** channel lets the sender
run ahead until the buffer fills.

Receiving has a two-value form that tells you whether the channel is closed, and `range`
over a channel loops until it is:

```go order
ch := make(chan int, 3)
ch <- 1
close(ch)
v, ok := <-ch
fmt.Println(v, ok)
```

Reading from a closed channel yields the zero value with `ok == false` — it does not
block and does not panic. *Sending* to a closed channel panics, which is why the rule is
that **the sender closes**, never the receiver.

> [!NOTE]
> **"Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating."** The most
> quoted Go proverb, and it is doing more work than it looks. The usual model is a shared
> variable plus a mutex, where the data sits still and the ownership is implied by whoever
> holds the lock. The channel model passes the *data* between goroutines, so at any moment
> exactly one of them has it, and ownership is a fact rather than a convention. It is not
> a rule that you must never use a mutex — the standard library is full of them, and
> `sync.Mutex` is often the simpler answer for guarding one counter. It is a claim about
> which model to reach for first.

### The runtime notices when everyone is asleep

```go
func main() {
	ch := make(chan int)
	<-ch
}
```

```
fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

goroutine 1 [chan receive]:
main.main()
	/path/dead.go:5 +0x25
exit status 2
```

Nothing can ever send on that channel, so nothing can ever wake `main`. The scheduler
notices that *every* goroutine is blocked, declares deadlock, and prints where each one is
stuck. Anyone who has attached gdb to a hung C++ process to work out which thread is
holding what will appreciate getting this for free.

The honest caveat: it only fires when **all** goroutines are asleep. One goroutine stuck
forever while the rest of the program hums along is not a deadlock the runtime can detect,
and that is the most common real leak in production Go — a goroutine blocked on a channel
nobody will ever write to, holding its stack and everything it references, forever.

### Waiting for a group of them

```go order
var wg sync.WaitGroup
wg.Add(1)
go func() {
	defer wg.Done()
	fmt.Println("working")
}()
wg.Wait()
```

`Add` before you start, `Done` on the way out — via `defer`, so a panic still counts —
and `Wait` blocks until the counter hits zero.

### The race detector, which you should just use

Concurrency bugs are not deterministic, which is what makes them awful. Here is a thousand
goroutines each doing `total++`:

```
total: 963
total: 985
total: 953
```

Three runs, three wrong answers, no crash, no error. `total++` is read-modify-write, and
the increments interleave. Now build with `-race`:

```
$ go run -race race.go
==================
WARNING: DATA RACE
Read at 0x00c00009a078 by goroutine 10:
  main.main.func1()
      race.go:15 +0x84

Previous write at 0x00c00009a078 by goroutine 7:
  main.main.func1()
      race.go:15 +0x96
```

It names the address, both goroutines, and both source lines. It is not a static check —
it instruments memory access at runtime and only reports races that actually happen, so it
finds nothing in code you don't exercise. Run your tests with `-race` in CI and you will
catch things that would otherwise surface once a month in production. It is not free — on a lock-heavy
loop doing 1.6 million increments, the same binary took 107 ms normally and 750 ms under
`-race`, about **7x** — which is why it is a flag rather than the default. Measure it on
your own workload before assuming a number; the overhead tracks how much memory traffic
you do, not how long the program runs.

The fixes here are a `sync.Mutex` around the increment, `atomic.AddInt64`, or having each
goroutine send its result down a channel and summing in one place.

quiz.prompt: What is a goroutine, and how does it differ from an OS thread in cost and in what schedules it?

options.text: A coroutine that only switches at explicit yield points you write
options.why: You never write a yield. The runtime switches at function calls, channel operations and system calls, and since Go 1.14 it can preempt a goroutine asynchronously — so a tight loop with no calls in it no longer starves everything else.

options.text: A runtime-scheduled task multiplexed M:N onto a small pool of OS threads, costing about 2 KB of growable stack rather than the 8 MB an OS thread reserves
options.why: The numbers are the argument: 100,000 goroutines alive at once used roughly 2 KB of stack each on four OS threads. A pthread's default stack on Linux is 8 MB — four thousand times more — which is why C and C++ servers end up with thread pools and hand-rolled event loops, and why "one goroutine per connection" is a real design in Go rather than a naive one.

options.text: A green thread with a fixed small stack, which is why deep recursion fails early
options.why: The stack starts small but *grows*: the runtime allocates a bigger one, copies the frames and fixes up the pointers. That is only possible because Go can find and rewrite pointers to stack data — precisely what C cannot do, and why C stacks must be reserved large up front.

options.text: A lightweight OS thread created with `clone()`, scheduled by the kernel
options.why: Starting one is an allocation, not a system call, and the kernel never sees it. If the kernel scheduled them, 100,000 of them would mean 100,000 schedulable entities rather than the four threads actually in use.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between an unbuffered and a buffered Go channel, and what synchronisation does an unbuffered one give you for free?

options.text: Unbuffered channels can hold one value; buffered ones hold many
options.why: An unbuffered channel holds nothing at all. There is no slot — the value passes directly from sender to receiver, which is what makes it a rendezvous rather than a queue of size one.

options.text: Unbuffered is a rendezvous — sender and receiver both block until the other arrives — so a completed send proves the handoff happened, with no mutex needed
options.why: The blocking *is* the synchronisation. A buffered channel breaks that guarantee deliberately: the sender may run ahead until the buffer fills, so a completed send proves only that there was room, not that anyone received. Choosing between them is choosing whether you need the handoff or the slack.

options.text: Unbuffered channels are faster because they skip the queue
options.why: Usually the opposite: an unbuffered send must wait for a receiver, so throughput is often lower. You choose unbuffered for the guarantee, not the speed.

options.text: Buffered channels are safe for concurrent use; unbuffered ones need a mutex
options.why: Both are safe for concurrent use by any number of goroutines — that is the point of the type. Neither needs an external lock.

quiz.prompt: In Go, who is supposed to close a channel, and what happens if you send on one that is already closed?

options.text: Either may close; sending afterwards is simply a no-op
options.why: It is not a no-op — it panics, and a panic in a goroutine with no recover takes the whole process down.

options.text: Channels must always be closed, or the program leaks
options.why: Closing is optional. A channel nobody references is garbage collected like anything else; close is a *signal* to receivers, not a resource release. The real leak is a goroutine blocked forever on a channel, not an unclosed channel.

options.text: The sender closes; sending on a closed channel panics, while receiving from one yields the zero value immediately with `ok == false`
options.why: The asymmetry is what forces the convention. A receiver cannot safely close, because a sender might still be about to send and would panic. A closed channel is perfectly usable for reading — `v, ok := <-ch` gives `0, false`, and `range` over it simply ends — so closing is how you say "no more values are coming".

options.text: The receiver closes, to signal it has stopped listening
options.why: That is exactly the mistake the panic exists to punish. To tell a sender to stop, you use a second channel or a `context`, not a close on the channel it is writing to.

quiz.prompt: The Go runtime reports `all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. What condition triggers that, and which very common concurrency bug does it fail to catch?

options.text: Two goroutines each holding a lock the other wants; it misses single-goroutine deadlocks
options.why: The runtime makes no attempt at lock-order analysis — it does not know what a cycle is. It only observes that nothing is runnable. A single goroutine receiving from an empty channel in `main` triggers it perfectly well.

options.text: Every single goroutine is blocked with nothing able to wake any of them — so it misses the far more common case of one goroutine stuck forever while the rest of the program runs on
options.why: The check is global, which makes it both reliable and limited. One goroutine blocked on a channel nobody will ever write to is invisible to it, and that is the most common real leak in production Go: the goroutine holds its stack and everything it references, forever, while the service looks perfectly healthy.

options.text: Any goroutine blocking for more than a few seconds; it misses fast deadlocks
options.why: There is no timeout involved. Blocking for hours is completely normal and reported as nothing, so long as something somewhere is still runnable.

options.text: A goroutine blocked on a mutex; it misses channel deadlocks
options.why: Backwards on both halves — the classic demonstration is a channel receive, and channel operations are exactly what the scheduler tracks.

quiz.prompt: A Go program with 1000 goroutines each doing `total++` on a shared variable prints a different wrong number every run and never crashes. What is happening, and what finds it?

options.text: `total++` is a read-modify-write whose steps interleave, losing increments — and `go run -race` instruments memory accesses at runtime and names both conflicting lines
options.why: Three runs gave 963, 985 and 953 out of 1000. Nothing crashes because nothing is corrupt in a way the hardware objects to; increments are simply lost. The race detector reports the address, both goroutines and both source lines. It is dynamic, not static, so it only sees races on code you actually execute — which is the argument for running your test suite under it in CI.

options.text: The compiler optimised the increment; building with `-N` fixes it
options.why: Disabling optimisation changes nothing here: the race is between goroutines, not an artefact of codegen. The fixes are a mutex, an atomic add, or sending each contribution down a channel and summing in one place.

options.text: The goroutines have not finished; adding a `WaitGroup` fixes the count
options.why: A tempting misreading, and worth ruling out deliberately: the demonstration already waits for every goroutine. Waiting correctly and still getting 963 is what proves the problem is the increment itself.

options.text: Go's memory model allows stale reads until a channel operation synchronises; `-race` cannot see it
options.why: The first clause gestures at something real — the memory model does define visibility in terms of happens-before edges — but the conclusion is wrong. This is exactly what the race detector is built to find, and it finds it immediately.
